desc:
You climb a staircase of n steps starting from the ground. In one move you may climb any number of steps from 1 to k (inclusive). You must land exactly on step n.

Return the number of different move sequences that take you to the top, modulo 1,000,000,007. Different orders count as different sequences.

Examples: n = 4, k = 2 gives 5, n = 4, k = 3 gives 7.
hints: The count for step i is the sum of the counts of the k steps below it. Computing that sum from scratch costs O(k) per step, which is too slow when k is large.
Neighbouring windows share almost all their elements: the window for i + 1 is the window for i with one value added and one removed.
Keep a running sum of ways over the last k steps. When moving to the next step add the newest value and subtract the one that just fell out of the window (remember the modulus).
editorial: Define ways(i) as the number of sequences landing exactly on step i, with ways(0) = 1. Then ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ... + ways(i-k) (terms with a negative index are 0). Evaluating every sum naively costs O(n · k), up to 1010 here.

Note that ways(i+1) = ways(i) + (ways(i) - ways(i-k)): the window sum for i+1 is the window sum for i plus the new value minus the value that left. Keeping the window sum S and updating it once per step gives O(n) time and O(n) space (the table is needed to know which value leaves the window). Apply the modulus to the subtraction carefully so S stays non-negative.
solution:
def countClimbsUpToK(n, k):
    M = 1000000007
    ways = [0] * (n + 1)
    ways[0] = 1
    window = 1                    # sum of ways[i-k .. i-1] for the current i, starting at i = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        ways[i] = window
        window = (window + ways[i] - (ways[i - k] if i - k >= 0 else 0)) % M
    return ways[n]
